---
title: "Reference selection"
subtitle: "Module 2 — 30 min"
---

## Why it matters

Reads are mapped to **one** reference, and the consensus is built from that mapping. A reference that is too
divergent makes reads map badly (or not at all), hides real variants and **biases the consensus towards the reference**.

| Criterion | Question |
|---|---|
| Same species / genotype | is it the right virus, the right genotype, the right segment? |
| Close to your samples | fewer differences = better mapping |
| Complete and good quality | no gaps, no ambiguous bases |
| Well documented | accession number, source, date |
| Consistent across the study | the **same** reference for all the samples you compare |

## Step 1 — Look at the three candidates

Three candidate references are in `data/reference/candidates/`:

- `TOYV1_TV1`: the original (root) genotype;
- `TOYV1_TV2`: a genotype that appeared later (8 mutations);
- `TOYV2_divergent`: another, more distant virus (about 8 % different).

```bash
seqkit stats data/reference/candidates/*.fasta
```

## Step 2 — Which one is closest to S01?

We count the differences between your S01 consensus and each candidate (positions with N are ignored):

```bash
python3 scripts/10_pick_reference.py results/consensus/S01.fa
```

(Plan B: `precomputed/consensus/S01.fa`. This small script is written for the course; in real life you would use
a BLAST or Nextclade search against a database.)

**Questions:** which reference is the closest? How many mismatches? Is it what you expected?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer
| Candidate | Compared sites | Mismatches | Identity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TOYV1_TV2** | 9,937 | **2** | 99.98 % |
| TOYV1_TV1 | 9,937 | 10 | 99.90 % |
| TOYV2_divergent | 9,937 | 807 | 91.88 % |

**TOYV1_TV2** is the closest: S01 carries the 8 lineage mutations of TV.2 and only 2 private ones, so it differs by 2 positions
from that reference and by 10 from the root. The divergent virus is ~8 % different: it is another virus and unusable here.
(Choosing between TV.1 and TV.2 changes little, but choosing the wrong virus changes everything.)
:::

## Step 3 — See the effect of a bad reference

Map S01 to the divergent reference and compare with the good mapping:

```bash
bwa index data/reference/candidates/TOYV2_divergent.fasta
```
```bash
bwa mem -t 2 data/reference/candidates/TOYV2_divergent.fasta results/trimmed/S01_R1.fastq.gz results/trimmed/S01_R2.fastq.gz \
  | samtools sort -o results/bam/S01_divergent.bam -
```
```bash
samtools flagstat results/bam/S01_divergent.bam
```

**Question:** what changes compared with `results/bam/S01.flagstat.txt`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer
With about 8 % divergence, a 150-base read has around 12 mismatches: fewer reads align (the exact % depends on the aligner),
many alignments are **soft-clipped** (only part of the read aligns) and the reads that do map carry dozens of false
differences. In IGV you would see a mosaic of coloured mismatches, and the consensus would be unreliable. The lesson:
**check that the reference is close to your virus before mapping**.
:::

## Final question

Why should all the samples of an outbreak be mapped to the **same** reference?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer
Because the differences are measured **against the reference**, with its coordinates. If each sample used another
reference, positions would not correspond, mutations would not be comparable, and differences between references would be
mistaken for differences between samples. One common reference = one common coordinate system = genomes you can align
and compare.
:::
